projects.title: Serverless Sales Analytics on AWS for a 50-Store Retailer
projects.tagline: A secure, pay-per-use AWS design that turns 50 stores' nightly sales files into one searchable history and weekly dashboards, for about CA$349 a month with all data kept in Canada.
projects.context: Cloud architecture business case, Sheridan College (October 2026)

dataset.name: RetailCo case scenario (course brief)
dataset.note: A fictional Canadian retailer described in the assignment brief: 50 stores, about 500 MB of point-of-sale CSV files a day, about 550 GB over three years. This project is a design and cost plan; it was not deployed.

projects.cover_alt: Fifty store dots feeding a numbered pipeline inside a dashed Canada region frame, ending in a dashboard

request.label: Request the full business case
request.intro: The full 8-page business case, the draw.io architecture diagram and the AWS Pricing Calculator estimate are available on request.
request.message: Hi Fathima, I'd like to see the full business case for your RetailCo AWS analytics architecture (diagram, service choices and cost estimate). Could you send it over?

projects.business_problem: RetailCo, a Canadian retailer with 50 stores in Ontario and British Columbia, gets about 500 MB of sales files from its tills every day, but they sit as separate daily exports. There is no single place to keep three years of history or to look at all stores together, and customer data has to stay private and in Canada.

highlights.label: A month to run
highlights.note: 30% under the CA$500 budget, in year 3

blocks.title: 50 stores, 50 files a night, and no one place to look
blocks.text: Every night, each of RetailCo's 50 stores exports its sales as a CSV file from the till (POS) system. That's about 500 MB a day, or about 550 GB over three years, but the files sit separately, so there is no single place to keep the history or compare stores. The system is only used a few times a day, so RetailCo should pay for what it uses, not for servers sitting idle.

visual.from: 50 stores, one file each a night
visual.alt: Fifty store icons sending files into one shared store of sales history

blocks.title: Six things the solution had to do
blocks.text: I started from RetailCo's requirements and checked every service choice and the cost estimate against them.

chips.text: Keep 3 years of sales history, available any time
Let analysts run their own queries (top products by region and store)
Keep the cost under CA$500 a month
Only authorized analysts see raw data

blocks.title: Follow one night of sales data
blocks.intro: My design is a serverless data lake in the Canada (Central) region. Press play, or select a step to see what happens there.

steps.name: Upload
steps.text: Each store runs a scheduled script every night that uploads the day's CSV file to Amazon S3 over HTTPS. Its IAM role can only add files to its own store folder. I chose this over AWS Transfer Family (SFTP), which would cost about US$217 a month just to receive 50 small files.

steps.name: Store
steps.text: The files land in the raw/ folder of one S3 bucket and are never changed, so they are the permanent record. I chose S3 over a database like RDS because the data is just files added daily and read in bulk, and S3 only charges for the space used.

steps.name: Clean
steps.text: Every night, an AWS Glue job cleans the new files, hides customer details and saves them as compressed Parquet files in curated/, split by year, month and day. It runs about 15 minutes and costs about US$6.60 a month.

steps.name: Catalogue
steps.text: A Glue Crawler then finds the new day's data and updates the Glue Data Catalog, the list of tables that Athena reads.

steps.name: Query
steps.text: Analysts use Amazon Athena to run SQL directly on the Parquet files, for example top products by region. Athena charges only for the data each query scans (about US$5.50 per TB), so the estimated 3 TB a month costs about US$16.

steps.name: Dashboards
steps.text: Once a week, Amazon QuickSight loads a summary from Athena and refreshes the dashboards. The three analysts build them as Authors.

steps.name: View
steps.text: The 50 store managers sign in to QuickSight as Readers. They see their weekly dashboard but have no access to S3 or Athena, so they never see raw customer data.

guard.label: Step 8 · Protect: security around every step

items.name: IAM
items.text: roles give each person only the access they need

blocks.title: The key decisions, and what I said no to
blocks.intro: For each part, I compared the obvious option with a simpler, cheaper one that still met every requirement.

items.title: Pay per question, not per hour
items.why: Redshift charges for every hour it runs, even when no one is using it. RetailCo only runs a few queries a day, so Athena's pay-per-query pricing is much cheaper.

items.title: Pack the data before searching it
items.why: Parquet stores data by column and compresses it, so Athena reads only what a query needs instead of scanning all 550 GB of CSV. Less data scanned means cheaper, faster queries.

items.title: No machines to babysit
items.why: EMR is a cluster that someone has to size, start and stop. Glue is serverless and bills by the second, which suits 500 MB a day.
items.number_label: a month for the nightly job

items.title: Files stay files
items.why: RDS charges for a database server running all day and needs the files loaded into tables first. S3 stores the files as they are, and Athena reads them in place.

items.title: Don't spend half the budget on the front door
items.why: An SFTP endpoint costs about US$0.30 an hour, almost half the budget just to receive 50 small files. A scheduled HTTPS upload costs almost nothing.

items.title: Dashboards that live next to the data
items.why: QuickSight connects to Athena directly, works with IAM and runs in Canada. Power BI and Tableau need separate licences and a connector. Readers cost US$3 a month each.

items.title: History on tap, not in the archive
items.why: Glacier is cheaper but can take hours to return data, and RetailCo needs its history available any time.

items.title: A second lock on the data
items.why: With SSE-S3, anyone who can read the bucket can read the files. With SSE-KMS you also need permission to use the key, and every use is logged.

items.title: No passwords lying around
items.why: Roles give temporary credentials instead of permanent access keys that could leak. Analysts also need MFA.

blocks.title: Does it fit the budget?
blocks.intro: I built the estimate in the AWS Pricing Calculator with every service in Canada (Central), sized for year 3, when all three years of data are stored.
blocks.verdict: Yes: US$248.94 a month (about CA$349 at 1.40), CA$151 (30%) under budget.
blocks.parts_title: Where the money goes (US$ a month)
blocks.parts_note: QuickSight seats are about 82% of the bill, so the cost depends on the number of users, not the amount of data. To control costs: an AWS Budgets alert at CA$400, a scan limit per query in Athena, and moving older raw files to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days.

compare.title: Why packing the data matters (Athena, US$ a month)
compare.note: Same 100 queries a day. The raw-CSV figure is my estimate: each query scanning all 550 GB at US$5.50 per TB.

blocks.title: Who can see what
blocks.intro: Four IAM roles, none with permanent keys. Each role gets only the access it needs, and store managers only see dashboards.

rows.note: can only add files to raw/

blocks.note: The S3 bucket policy also blocks any request that isn't HTTPS or isn't encrypted with KMS, and Block Public Access stays on.

blocks.title: Who is responsible for security?
blocks.intro: Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, AWS and RetailCo each secure a different part.

columns.title: Security of the cloud
items: Data centres in the Canada (Central) region
The servers behind Glue, Athena and QuickSight

columns.title: Security in the cloud
items: Choosing ca-central-1 before any data is uploaded
Writing the IAM, bucket and key policies
Turning on encryption and managing the key
Deciding who is an authorized analyst

blocks.title: Did it work? Every requirement, met

items.need: Three years of history, available any time
items.how: S3 Standard keeps every file with instant access; Parquet copies keep queries fast as history grows.

items.need: Analysts can ask their own questions
items.how: Athena runs SQL on the Glue Data Catalog tables; partitions and Parquet keep each query small.
QuickSight dashboards refresh weekly from Athena; managers are Readers.
About CA$349 a month in year 3, because every service is pay-per-use.
Every resource, including Athena results and QuickSight, is in ca-central-1. Trade-offs I accepted: Athena costs about 10% more there and some QuickSight AI features aren't available.

items.need: Only approved analysts see raw data
items.how: IAM roles, the bucket policy, the KMS key policy and CloudTrail logging.

blocks.title: The original work
blocks.intro: The architecture diagram I drew in draw.io with the official AWS icons, and my AWS Pricing Calculator estimate.

items.alt: AWS architecture diagram: stores upload to Amazon S3 in the Canada Central region; AWS Glue transforms and catalogues the data; Amazon Athena queries it; Amazon QuickSight serves dashboards to store managers; IAM, KMS and CloudTrail secure every stage. Numbered badges 1 to 8 mark the steps.
items.caption: Architecture diagram, drawn in draw.io with the official AWS icons. Badges 1–8 match the steps above.

items.alt: AWS Pricing Calculator estimate for six services in Canada (Central): monthly total US$248.94, 12-month total US$2,987.28.
items.caption: AWS Pricing Calculator estimate: US$248.94 a month, all six services in Canada (Central).

insights: For a small, occasionally used workload, serverless pay-per-use services beat always-on servers on both cost and effort: nothing runs, and nothing is billed, while no one is asking questions.
How the data is stored decides what queries cost: packing it into partitioned Parquet keeps Athena around US$16 a month instead of thousands.
The biggest cost is people, not data: QuickSight seats are about 82% of the bill, so headcount, not data growth, is the number to watch.
Keeping data in Canada has small, known trade-offs (about 10% higher Athena pricing and some QuickSight AI features unavailable), and they are worth it for PIPEDA.
recommendations: Set an AWS Budgets alert at CA$400 so RetailCo is warned well before the CA$500 limit.
Add a per-query scan limit in the Athena workgroup so one careless query can't run up the bill.
Add an S3 Lifecycle rule to move raw files older than 90 days to S3 Standard-IA: cheaper, but still instant.
Review Amazon Redshift only if RetailCo grows to hundreds of daily dashboard users.
improvements: Build a small proof of concept in the AWS Learner Lab with sample data, to measure real Glue run times and Athena scan sizes against the estimates.
Add data-quality checks to the nightly job (row counts, missing stores, duplicate files) with an alert when a store's file doesn't arrive.
Orchestrate the job and crawler with AWS Glue Workflows or Step Functions instead of separate schedules.

projects.title: Rocky Mountain Bikes: Sales and Profit Analysis in Power BI
projects.tagline: A 4-page Power BI report on $110M of bike sales across three fiscal years. Sales more than doubled, but resellers earn almost no profit: online sales bring in 92% of it.
projects.context: Power BI course project, Sheridan College (October 2026)

dataset.name: Rocky Mountain Bikes sales data (course case-study dataset)
dataset.note: Five files in five formats: customers (CSV), products and resellers (Excel), territories (JSON) and sales orders (Access database). 121,253 order lines from July 2023 to June 2026; the fiscal year runs July to June.

projects.cover_alt: Three rising fiscal-year columns split into reseller and online sales, with a monthly sales line above

request.label: Request the Power BI report
request.intro: The .pbix report (4 pages), the data model and the DAX measures are available on request.
request.message: Hi Fathima, I'd like to see your Rocky Mountain Bikes Power BI report. Could you send the file or walk me through it?

projects.business_problem: Rocky Mountain Bikes (RMB) sells bikes, components, clothing and accessories online and through about 635 resellers. Management wanted to understand three years of sales (July 2023 to June 2026): what is growing, where the profit really comes from, and what may happen next year. The data was spread across five files in five different formats.

blocks.title: From five files to one report
blocks.intro: Select a step to see what was done there, or press play.

steps.name: Get data
steps.text: Connected to all five sources: Customers (CSV), Products and Resellers (Excel), Territories (JSON) and the sales orders (Access database, two tables).

steps.name: Clean
steps.text: Removed duplicate products and territories, dropped the Corporate HQ territory, trimmed text, labelled missing values (for example "N/A - Reseller Sale" instead of [Not Applicable]), merged the order header into the order lines, and added Sales Amount, Total Cost and Days to Ship columns.

steps.name: Model
steps.text: One Sales fact table (121,253 rows) linked to Customers, Products, Resellers, Territories and a fiscal-year Dates table (July to June). Order date is the active date link; ship date is an inactive one, used only when needed.

steps.name: Measure
steps.text: Total Sales, Gross Profit, Profit Margin %, Order Count, Average Order Value, Customer Count, Sales YoY Growth %, Sales Fiscal YTD, Average Discount % and Sales by Ship Date (USERELATIONSHIP), kept together in one measures table.

steps.name: Report
steps.text: Executive Overview, Profit by Product and Channel, Customers and Geography, and Trends and Forecast. Every page has fiscal-year and channel slicers and a one-line takeaway at the bottom.

projects.visuals_intro: Hover over any chart to see the numbers, or switch to the table view. All values are recalculated from the report's data model.

charts.title: Sales by fiscal year and channel
charts.caption: Sales grew 42% in FY2025 and 53% in FY2026. Online sales dipped in FY2025, then more than doubled in FY2026.

charts.title: Share of sales vs share of profit
charts.caption: Resellers bring in almost three quarters of sales but less than 8% of the profit. Online sales earn a 41% margin; reseller sales earn 1.2%.

charts.title: Monthly sales, July 2023 to June 2026
charts.caption: A clear upward trend with a strong seasonal pattern: November, May, August and September are the busiest months; January and October are the slowest.

charts.title: Sales by region (all three years)
charts.caption: North America brings in about 72% of sales. The US Southwest is the largest region; Germany is the smallest.

comparison.title: Online vs reseller sales (FY2024 to FY2026)
comparison.note: Online customers pay list price. Resellers get about 41% off on average, which wipes out the margin: bikes sold through resellers lose money overall (-0.7% margin).

subprojects.title: 1. Overview
subprojects.description: The one-page summary for management.
steps: KPI cards: Total Sales, Gross Profit, Profit Margin % and Order Count
Sales by fiscal year and channel (column chart) and share of sales by channel (pie)
Gross profit and margin by fiscal year (combo chart) and sales by product category (bar)

chart.title: Gross profit and margin by fiscal year

subprojects.key_insight: Sales more than doubled in two years, but the profit margin fell from 13.2% in FY2024 to 11.8% in FY2026. Resellers and bikes drive most of the sales.

subprojects.title: 2. Profit
subprojects.description: Where RMB makes money and where it loses it.
steps: KPI cards: Units Sold, Average Discount % and Gross Profit
Sales by category with drill-down to subcategory
Profit margin by category, Internet vs Reseller
Gross profit by subcategory, with losses in red, and a reseller scatter of sales vs margin

chart.title: Profit margin by category and channel

subprojects.key_insight: Bikes sell well, but reseller discounts are so large that RMB loses money on bikes sold through resellers. Jerseys, touring frames and caps lose money overall. (Components are sold only through resellers, at an 8.8% margin.)

subprojects.title: 3. Customers
subprojects.description: Where sales come from, and who is buying online.
steps: KPI cards: Customer Count and Average Order Value
Sales by territory and channel (bar chart)
Decomposition tree: break sales down by group, country, region, channel and category
Top 10 online customers (table) and online customers per fiscal year (column chart)
subprojects.key_insight: North America brings in about 72% of sales. Online customers grew about five-fold in FY2026, from 3,394 to 17,587.

subprojects.title: 4. Trends and forecast
subprojects.description: What is changing over time, and what FY2027 may look like.
steps: KPI cards: Sales Fiscal YTD and Average Days to Ship (7 days)
Monthly sales with a 12-month Power BI forecast for FY2027
Monthly sales pattern compared year over year
Orders vs average order value (combo chart) and year-over-year sales growth

chart.title: Orders up, average order value down

subprojects.key_insight: Orders jumped from 4,776 to 23,469 in FY2026 while the average order value fell from about $7,150 to $2,220: many more, smaller online orders. If the trend continues, FY2027 sales will grow again.

insights: Sales grew from $24.1M (FY2024) to $52.1M (FY2026), up 42% and then 53%, but the profit margin slipped from 13.2% to 11.8%.
Resellers bring in 73% of sales but only about 8% of gross profit (1.2% margin), because they buy at about 41% below list price.
Online sales are 27% of sales but 92% of gross profit, at a 41% margin.
Bikes are 86% of sales. Through resellers, bikes lose money overall (-0.7% margin), and 329 of 635 resellers (52%) are unprofitable.
Online customers grew about five-fold in FY2026 (3,394 to 17,587), bringing many smaller orders: average order value fell from about $7,150 to $2,220.
North America is 72% of sales; the US Southwest alone is $24.3M. Sales peak in November, May, August and September.
recommendations: Review reseller pricing: cap discounts, especially on bikes, so reseller sales are at least break-even.
Grow the online channel, which earns a 41% margin, for example with marketing in the busiest months.
Review the 329 unprofitable resellers and renegotiate terms with the largest ones first.
Fix or drop loss-making lines: jerseys, touring frames and caps.
Plan stock and staff around the peak months (November, May, August, September).
improvements: Add a profit-and-margin forecast, not only a sales forecast.
Add drill-through pages for a single reseller or product, with targets and variance.
Publish to the Power BI Service with row-level security, so each regional manager sees only their own territory.
approach: Get data: connected to five sources in five formats (CSV, Excel, JSON and an Access database).
Clean: Power Query steps to remove duplicates, trim text, label missing values, merge the order tables and add calculated columns.
Model: a star schema with one Sales fact table, four dimension tables and a fiscal-year Dates table.
Measure: 18 DAX measures, including time intelligence (year-over-year growth, fiscal year-to-date).
Report: four themed pages with slicers, drill-down, a decomposition tree, a forecast and a takeaway line on every page.

projects.title: Coffee Chain Store Performance Analysis
projects.tagline: Why do some of a coffee chain's 12 shops earn four times more than others? Descriptive statistics, correlation, regression and probability, across Excel, Python and R.

dataset.name: The Corner Cup store data (course case-study dataset)
dataset.note: A fictional chain of 12 coffee shops supplied for the course: location type, floor size, staff, daily customers, average spend per customer, monthly revenue and customer satisfaction. 12 rows and 8 columns, with no missing values.

projects.cover_alt: Scatter plot of the 12 shops with a rising regression line

request.label: Request the project files
request.intro: The Excel workbook, Python notebook, R script and full written report are available on request.
request.message: Hi Fathima, I'd like to see more of your coffee chain store performance analysis (the Excel workbook, Python notebook and R script). Could you share them?

projects.business_problem: The owner of The Corner Cup runs 12 coffee shops, 7 in the city and 5 in the suburbs, and has big decisions ahead: which shops to grow, which need help, and where to open next. Revenue ranges from $32.3K to $131K a month. The question was what actually drives that gap, and what she should do about it.

highlights.label: Daily customers and revenue
highlights.note: The strongest link in the data

highlights.label: Of revenue differences explained
highlights.note: Regression on daily customers, R² = 0.77, p < 0.001

highlights.label: Monthly revenue per extra daily customer

approach: Excel: frequency table, summary statistics and coefficient of variation, then an urban vs suburban comparison with a two-sample t-test.
Python: loaded and checked the data with pandas, built a histogram, scatter plot and box plot, and a correlation matrix with a heat map.
R: fitted a simple linear regression of revenue on daily customers, predicted revenue for a new 300-customer shop, and answered planning questions with the binomial and Poisson distributions.
Turned the results into three recommendations for the owner, each with its evidence and a concrete action.
projects.visuals_intro: Hover over any chart to see each shop's numbers, or switch to the table view. All values are calculated from the 12-shop dataset.

charts.title: Daily customers vs monthly revenue
charts.caption: Busier shops earn more: each point is a shop and the dashed line is the regression fit. Airport Terminal (441 customers a day) sits about $27.5K below the line because its customers spend the least, while suburban Tech Campus earns more than most city shops.

charts.title: Monthly revenue by shop
charts.caption: Revenue ranges from $32.3K to $131K, about four times apart. Only 4 of the 12 shops earn more than $80K a month.

charts.title: What moves with revenue? (correlation, r)
charts.caption: Foot traffic stands out. The other four factors move together (bigger, better-staffed shops with higher spend and happier customers) but bigger shops do not attract more customers. Correlation shows a link, not cause and effect.

comparison.title: Urban vs suburban shops (averages)
comparison.note: City shops earn more because they are busier, not because customers spend more or are happier. The revenue gap is not statistically significant (Welch t-test, p = 0.071), so location type alone does not decide success.

projects.tabs_title: How it was done, tool by tool

subprojects.title: Excel: describe the data
subprojects.description: Descriptive statistics in an Excel workbook, built with formulas so every number can be traced.
steps: COUNTIF frequency table and bar chart of urban and suburban shops (7 and 5)
AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, MIN and MAX, plus the coefficient of variation to compare spread across units
AVERAGEIF group averages and a two-tailed T.TEST for the urban vs suburban revenue gap

chart.title: How much each measure varies (coefficient of variation)

subprojects.key_insight: Revenue and daily customers vary a lot from shop to shop, while spend per customer and satisfaction stay fairly steady. That pointed to foot traffic as the main source of the revenue gap.

subprojects.title: Python: visualise and correlate
subprojects.description: Exploration and charts in a Python notebook with pandas and matplotlib.
steps: Loaded the CSV with pandas and checked it with head(), info() and describe(); results matched Excel
Histogram of revenue, scatter plot of customers vs revenue by location, and box plot of satisfaction
Correlation matrix with data.corr() and a heat map
subprojects.key_insight: Revenue is slightly right-skewed (skewness 0.63): most shops earn $32K to $98K and Harbour View stands alone at $131K. Daily customers correlate with revenue at r = 0.88, far more than any other factor.

subprojects.title: R: regression and probability
subprojects.description: Modelling and probability questions in an R script, run in RStudio.
steps: lm(Monthly_Revenue_000 ~ Daily_Customers): Revenue ($000) = −2.785 + 0.276 × Daily customers, R² = 0.768
Predicted a new 300-customer shop at about $80.0K a month (95% prediction interval $47.3K to $112.7K)
Binomial model for 5 new suburban shops (40% chance each of becoming high-revenue) and a Poisson model of Airport Terminal arrivals (18 an hour)

chart.title: Of 5 new shops, how many become high-revenue? (binomial, p = 0.4)

subprojects.key_insight: About 2 of 5 new suburban shops should do well, with a 92.2% chance that at least one does and a 7.8% chance that none do. At the airport, a rush of 25 or more customers an hour happens about 6.8% of the time, roughly 1.6 hours a day.

insights: Foot traffic drives revenue: daily customers explain about 77% of the differences between shops (R² = 0.77), and each extra customer a day adds about $276 a month.
City shops earn $83.3K a month against $54.9K in the suburbs, but mainly because they are busier. Spend and satisfaction are almost the same, and the gap is not statistically significant (p = 0.071).
Airport Terminal is the busiest shop (441 a day) but has the lowest spend ($6.90) and satisfaction (3.5), and earns about $27.5K less than the model predicts.
Only 4 of 12 shops earn more than $80K a month, so the chance that a shop is high-revenue is 1 in 3.
recommendations: Choose new sites by foot traffic, not by the urban or suburban label. Count pedestrian traffic before signing a lease and aim for about 300 customers a day, the level the model links to an $80K shop.
Raise spend per customer at the Airport Terminal with combo deals and quick add-ons ($1 more per customer is about $13,000 a month), and add staff for the 25-plus-customer peaks.
Open new suburban shops in stages: 2 or 3 high-traffic sites first, review after 6 to 12 months, then decide on the rest.
improvements: With only 12 shops at one point in time, every estimate has wide uncertainty. Monthly data over a year would show trends and seasonality.
A multiple regression with daily customers and spend per customer together would likely explain much of the remaining 23%.
An interactive Power BI dashboard would let the owner explore each shop herself.
